cards.front: You ran `git reset --hard HEAD~1` by mistake. To undo it, should you run `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}` or `git reset --hard HEAD~1`?
cards.back: `git reset --hard HEAD@{1}`. Running `HEAD~1` again would drop another commit.

cards.front: You ran `git reset --hard` while you had uncommitted edits in `etl.py`. Can `git reflog` bring those edits back?
cards.back: No. The reflog only lists commits that HEAD and branches pointed to, and your edits were never in a commit.

cards.front: You commit an AWS key, then delete it in the next commit. Is the key gone from the repository?
cards.back: No, the old commit still contains it, and anyone with the repo can read it from history.commit 1: key addedcommit 2: key deletedhistory keeps commit 1still readable

cards.front: You rewrite history and force-push to remove a leaked key. Why must you still rotate the key?
cards.back: Anyone who cloned, forked or scanned the repo before the rewrite may already have a copy.

cards.front: Is a bad rebase permanent once it finishes?
cards.back: No. The old commits still exist for a while; `git reflog` shows them so you can reset back.

cards.front: What does it mean to rotate a leaked secret?
cards.back: Create a new secret, switch your apps to it, then disable the old one so it stops working.

cards.front: You deleted the branch `feature` with `git branch -D`. Its own reflog is gone too. Where do you look for its last commit?
cards.back: Run `git reflog`, find the last commit you made on `feature`, then run `git branch feature <hash>`.

cards.front: During a rebase conflict, what do `ours` and `theirs` refer to?
cards.back: They are swapped compared to a merge: `ours` is the branch you rebase onto, `theirs` is your commit.`ours``theirs`Mergeyour current branchbranch being merged inRebasebranch rebased ontoyour commit being replayed

You reset away a commit two months ago and never referenced it again. Why might `git reflog` no longer show it?
cards.back: Reflog entries for unreachable commits expire after 30 days by default. After that, `git gc` can delete the commit for good.

cards.front: After rebasing a pushed branch, why use `git push --force-with-lease` instead of `--force`?
cards.back: It refuses to overwrite the remote if someone pushed commits you have not fetched, so their work survives.

cards.front: A key was pushed to a private repository. Why is it still considered leaked?
cards.back: Everyone with access, every clone on a laptop, and any future copy of the repo can read it.

cards.front: Why should you not rebase a branch that teammates have already pulled?
cards.back: Rebase replaces its commits with new ones, so teammates' copies no longer match and they get duplicates or conflicts.

cards.front: You force-pushed and wiped out a teammate's commit on the remote. Can you find their commit with `git reflog` in your clone?
cards.back: Only if your clone once had that commit. Otherwise the teammate must recover it from their own reflog.

cards.front: Why can a rebase make you fix the same conflict several times, when a merge asks only once?
cards.back: Rebase replays your commits one at a time, so each commit touching those lines can conflict again.

cards.front: A file with a password is already committed. Does adding it to `.gitignore` stop Git tracking it?
cards.back: No, `.gitignore` only affects untracked files; the committed file stays tracked and in history.
